claim: Working memory is the cognitive capacity of short-term storage of information for goal-directed behaviors.
source: Working memory is the cognitive capacity of short-term storage of information for goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of cognitive neuroscience.

claim: Auditory cortex stores information by persistent changes of neural activity.
source: We show that auditory cortex stores information by persistent changes of neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the studies described in the manuscript.

claim: Working memory was reflected in the spiking activity of individual neurons in auditory cortex.
source: Working memory was reflected in the spiking activity of individual neurons in auditory cortex and in the activity of neuronal populations, that is, in local field potentials and magnetic fields.
evidence: This claim is supported by spike activity recordings from monkey auditory cortex presented in the manuscript.

claim: Working memory was reflected in local field potentials in auditory cortex.
source: Working memory was reflected in the spiking activity of individual neurons in auditory cortex and in the activity of neuronal populations, that is, in local field potentials and magnetic fields.
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recordings from monkey auditory cortex presented in the manuscript.

claim: Working memory was reflected in magnetic fields in auditory cortex.
source: Working memory was reflected in the spiking activity of individual neurons in auditory cortex and in the activity of neuronal populations, that is, in local field potentials and magnetic fields.
evidence: This claim is supported by MEG recordings from human subjects presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar working memory-related activity was observed in humans and monkeys.
source: Because similar activity was observed in the two species, the cellular bases of some auditory working memory processes in humans can be studied in monkeys.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing results from human MEG studies and monkey electrophysiology studies in the manuscript.

claim: The cellular bases of some auditory working memory processes in humans can be studied in monkeys.
source: Because similar activity was observed in the two species, the cellular bases of some auditory working memory processes in humans can be studied in monkeys.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of similar working memory-related activity in both species.

claim: Working memory arises through the coordinated recruitment, via attention, of brain areas in a broad network.
source: It is further assumed that WM arises through the coordinated recruitment, via attention, of brain areas in a broad network (Constantinidis and Procyk, 2004; Postle, 2006; Ranganath and D'Esposito, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Task-relevant information is stored in some of the same brain areas that also process it, such as sensory cortex.
source: and that the task-relevant information is stored in some of the same brain areas that also process it, such as sensory cortex, whereas prefrontal cortex (PFC) is thought to aid storage of the information in sensory cortex (D'Esposito, 2007; Postle, 2006; Sreenivasan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prefrontal cortex is thought to aid storage of information in sensory cortex.
source: and that the task-relevant information is stored in some of the same brain areas that also process it, such as sensory cortex, whereas prefrontal cortex (PFC) is thought to aid storage of the information in sensory cortex (D'Esposito, 2007; Postle, 2006; Sreenivasan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Auditory cortex is involved in the performance of auditory working memory tasks.
source: In the auditory modality, lesion (Colombo et al., 1990, 1996; Fritz et al., 2005), imaging (Brechmann et al., 2007; Grimault et al., 2014; Guimond et al., 2011; Kumar et al., 2016; Linke and Cusack, 2015; Linke et al., 2011; Nolden et al., 2013; Rämä et al., 2004), and recording studies (Bigelow et al., 2014; Gottlieb et al., 1989; Sakurai, 1994; Scott et al., 2014) have revealed that auditory cortex (AC) is involved in the performance of auditory WM tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies using different methodologies.

claim: Neural activity in auditory cortex is persistently elevated or suppressed during the period when information needs to be held in working memory.
source: Although some of these studies have demonstrated neural activity in AC that is persistently elevated or suppressed during the period when information needs to be held in WM, we argue here that such persistent changes in activity do not unequivocally reflect WM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies, though the authors argue these findings are not unequivocal.

claim: Many studies have not controlled for potential long-lasting neural activity evoked by a stimulus and for mental processes other than working memory.
source: Many studies have not controlled for potential long-lasting neural activity evoked by a stimulus and for mental processes other than WM that are associated with performing a task, such as general attention, reward expectation or preparation for behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous research methodology based on the authors' analysis of the literature.

claim: Mental processes such as general attention, reward expectation or preparation for behavioral responses can be associated with changes in auditory cortex activity that last for seconds.
source: These processes can also be associated with changes in AC activity that last for seconds (Brosch et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In task 1, sources in the left and right auditory cortex were significantly stronger in high- than in low-WM-load trials during the final 500 ms of the delay.
source: In addition, sources in the left and right AC were significantly stronger in high- (thick orange traces) than in low-WM-load trials (thin blue traces) during the final 500 ms of the delay (p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, permutation test; for p-values, see the numbers above the abscissae in Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: The peak source strengths around the time of the M100 were very similar in high- and low-WM-load trials in task 1.
source: In contrast, the peak source strengths around the time of the M100, the most prominent component of the early responses evoked by the two different S1s, were very similar in the high- and low-WM-load trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by MEG data analysis from task 1.

claim: In task 3, differences in source strength between go and nogo trials were not significant in the left or right auditory cortex.
source: In this task, differences between go and nogo trials were not significant (p>0.05, permutation test), neither in the left AC (Figure 2e) nor in the right AC (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data shown in Figure 2e,f.

claim: The differences in source strength between high- and low-WM-load trials in tasks 1 and 2 were due to differences in working memory load but not due to differences in preparatory activity or late activity.
source: It is likely that the differences in source strength between the high- and low-WM-load trials in tasks 1 and 2 were due to differences in WM load but presumably not due to differences in preparatory activity or late activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing results of tasks 1, 2, and 3.

claim: In both auditory cortices, the sources were stronger in task 4 than in task 5 during the entire delay.
source: In addition, in both ACs, the sources were stronger in task 4 than in task 5 during the entire delay, being significant during many portions of the delay (p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction, permutation test; for p values, see the numbers above the abscissae).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The peak source strengths during the M100 component evoked by S1 were very similar in tasks 4 and 5.
source: In contrast, the peak source strengths during the M100 component evoked by S1 were very similar in the two tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by MEG data analysis from tasks 4 and 5.

claim: The peak amplitude of the M100 component is strongly modulated by attention.
source: This suggests that levels of general attention in tasks 4 and 5 were similar during the presentation of S1 because the peak amplitude of the M100 component is strongly modulated by attention (Kauramäki et al., 2012; Woldorff et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The differences in source strengths during the delay between tasks 4 and 5 were due to differences in working memory load.
source: Because tasks 4 and 5 differed in WM load, but not in S1 or in the proportions of go and nogo trials, we conclude that the differences in source strengths during the delay between the two tasks were due to differences in WM load and that activity in both ACs can be related to WM.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design and data analysis.

claim: 27.4% and 34.5% of multiunits in monkey auditory cortex had high-/low-load spike-rate ratios significantly different from 1 during the delay in tasks 1 and 6, respectively.
source: Ratios significantly different from 1 (significant ratios) were obtained from 27.4% and 34.5% of the multiunits during the delay in tasks 1 and 6, respectively (green dots), with the majority of ratios >1 (71 of 84 in task 1; 99 of 106 in task 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The majority of significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios were greater than 1 in tasks 1 and 6.
source: Ratios significantly different from 1 (significant ratios) were obtained from 27.4% and 34.5% of the multiunits during the delay in tasks 1 and 6, respectively (green dots), with the majority of ratios >1 (71 of 84 in task 1; 99 of 106 in task 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data.

claim: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios occurred in only one of the two tasks in 65% of multiunits and in both tasks in 35% of multiunits.
source: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios occurred in only one of the two tasks in the majority of the units and in both tasks in the minority of the units (65% vs. 35% for multiunits and 92% vs. 8% for single units; Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike activity data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: 30.0% of multiunits and 21.7% of single units in core fields of auditory cortex exhibited working memory-related spike activity.
source: Thus, 30.0% (92/307) of the multiunits and 21.7% (33/152) of the single units in core fields of AC were considered to exhibit WM-related spike activity.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of spike activity data considering task and stimulus specificity.

claim: For the majority of multiunits, spike rates increased with increasing working memory load.
source: For the majority of multiunits, spike rates increased with increasing WM load (yielding ratios >1) and for the minority spike rates decreased with increasing WM load (yielding ratios <1; Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike activity data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed more often when monkeys performed the tasks correctly than when they made errors.
source: In both tasks, significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed more often (p<0.001, chi-square test, one-tailed) in multiunit recordings obtained when the monkeys performed the tasks correctly (27.4% in task 1 and 34.5% in task 6) than when they made errors (9.8% and 9.5%)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed more often when monkeys performed the tasks correctly than in passive conditions.
source: In both tasks, significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed more often (p<0.001, chi-square test, one-tailed) in multiunit recordings obtained when the monkeys performed the tasks correctly (27.4% in task 1 and 34.5% in task 6) than when they made errors (9.8% and 9.5%) or in the responses to the corresponding sequences recorded when the monkeys did not perform the tasks (5.5% and 7.5%; Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Delay enhancement clearly dominated over delay suppression in both tasks, most prominently in high-WM-load trials.
source: We also observed both persistent enhancement and suppression in core fields of AC but enhancement clearly dominated in both tasks, and most prominently in high-WM-load trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of delay/baseline spike-rate ratios shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The majority of significant delay/baseline spike-rate ratios were greater than 1 in both high- and low-WM-load trials.
source: In both high- and low-WM-load trials, and in both tasks, the majority of the significant delay/baseline ratios were >1 (Figure 4g).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike activity data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Differences in working memory load were reflected in local field potentials recorded in core fields of auditory cortex.
source: During the delay, differences in WM load were also reflected in the LFPs recorded in core fields of AC.
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recordings and analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Significant LFP differences occurred more frequently during the delay than during baseline.
source: Similar to the results obtained with spike activity, significant LFP differences occurred more frequently during the delay than during baseline (p<0.001, chi-square test, one-tailed).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The frequency of occurrence of significant LFP differences during the delay was significantly higher when monkeys performed the tasks correctly than when they made errors or in passive conditions.
source: The frequency of occurrence of significant LFP differences during the delay also depended on the behavioral context, being significantly higher (p<0.001, chi-square test, one-tailed) when the monkeys performed the tasks correctly (25.5% and 27.1% in tasks 1 and 6, respectively) than when they made errors (13.5% and 7.9%) or than in the responses to the corresponding sequences when the monkeys did not perform the tasks in the passive condition (8.3% and 9.3%; Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Significant LFP differences occurred in only one of the two tasks at 79% of sites and in both tasks at 21% of sites.
source: Also mirroring the spike activity, significant LFP differences occurred in only one of the two tasks at the majority of sites (107 of the 135 sites with a significant LFP difference in one or both tasks; 79%) and in both tasks at the minority of sites (28 of 135; 21%; Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of LFP data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: At 34.5% of sites, LFP differences between high- and low-WM-load trials were due to differences in working memory load.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that at 107 of 310 sites (34.5%) the LFP differences between high- and low-WM-load trials were due to differences in WM load.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from LFP data analysis considering task specificity.

claim: Negative delay–baseline LFP differences prevailed over positive ones in both high- and low-WM-load trials.
source: Figure 5g shows that negative delay–baseline LFP differences prevailed over positive ones in both high- (31.7% vs 29.1% in task 1; 41.7% vs 11.9% in task 6) and low-WM-load trials (38.0% vs 20.3% in task 1; 69.1% vs 4.8% in task 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of LFP data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: A similar proportion of multiunits in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex displayed high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay differing significantly from 1 compared to auditory cortex.
source: We observed that, compared to core fields of AC, a similar proportion of multiunits in vlPFC displayed high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay differing significantly from 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of spike activity data from auditory cortex and prefrontal cortex.

claim: In ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, suppression was as common as, or even more common than, enhancement during the delay.
source: Unlike in core fields of AC, where overall enhancement during the delay dominated and spike rates predominantly changed in high-WM-load trials (Figure 4f,g), in vlPFC suppression was as common as, or even more common than, enhancement during the delay (Figure 6d,f,g).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike activity data from prefrontal cortex shown in Figure 6.

claim: Differential latencies were significantly shorter in core fields of auditory cortex than in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, with a median difference of approximately 100 ms.
source: In both tasks, differential latencies were significantly shorter in core fields of AC than in vlPFC, with a median difference of ∼100 ms (p<0.001, permutation test, two-tailed).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of differential latencies shown in Figure 7.

claim: The finding that differential latencies were shorter in auditory cortex than in prefrontal cortex is difficult to reconcile with the notion that prefrontal cortex exerts a top-down modulation of activity in sensory cortex.
source: This finding is difficult to reconcile with the notion that PFC exerts a top-down modulation of activity in sensory cortex (Sreenivasan et al., 2014) and thus triggers the storage of information in core fields of AC on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential latency data and comparison with existing theories.

claim: Information is temporarily stored in auditory cortex by persistent changes in spike rates and slow potentials.
source: Our converging results from intracranial recordings in monkeys and extracranial recordings in humans demonstrated that information is temporarily stored in AC by persistent changes in spike rates and slow potentials.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from both monkey and human studies.

claim: Enhancement of activity in auditory cortex during the delay may serve to refresh representations of information to keep them active.
source: Enhancement of activity in AC during the delay may serve to refresh representations of information to keep them active while suppression of activity may serve to protect representations from internal or external interference (Linke et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Suppression of activity in auditory cortex may serve to protect representations from internal or external interference.
source: Enhancement of activity in AC during the delay may serve to refresh representations of information to keep them active while suppression of activity may serve to protect representations from internal or external interference (Linke et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The working memory-related activity in the core fields of auditory cortex was stimulus specific.
source: The WM-related activity in the core fields of AC, as measured in monkeys, was stimulus specific, i.e., it was observed only when a specific frequency of S1 (or specific stimulus-response associations of S2) had to be stored in WM.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike activity data showing task specificity.

claim: The results provide evidence for the sensory-recruitment hypothesis of working memory.
source: Our report provides evidence for the sensory-recruitment hypothesis of WM (Sreenivasan et al., 2014), which posits that storage of information recruits the same neurons in sensory cortex that represent the information.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results and comparison with existing theories.

claim: Single neurons in auditory cortex are capable of temporarily storing information by changing their spike rates.
source: Our results imply that single neurons in AC are capable of temporarily storing information by changing their spike rates.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the single-unit recording data.

claim: Neurons exhibiting enhancement or suppression during the delay are spatially organized in clusters.
source: It is conceivable that these neurons are spatially organized in clusters preferentially exhibiting either enhancement or suppression during the delay.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation that WM-related activity in multiunits was as common as in single units.

claim: Activity in both the left and right auditory cortex was related to working memory.
source: Our MEG studies clarified that activity in both the left and right AC was related to WM.
evidence: This claim is supported by MEG data from human subjects.

claim: Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex is involved in non-spatial auditory working memory tasks.
source: Such activity is consistent with previous studies showing that vlPFC is involved in non-spatial auditory WM tasks (Hwang and Romanski, 2015; Plakke and Romanski, 2014; Plakke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex stores information in the same ways as auditory cortex.
source: Although based on one monkey only, our observation of persistent enhancement and suppression of spike rates during the delay suggests that vlPFC stores information in the same ways as AC.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from spike activity data from prefrontal cortex, though the authors note it is based on one monkey.

claim: Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex does not trigger the storage of information in auditory cortex on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: Our observation that WM-related activity started ∼100 ms later in vlPFC than in AC suggests that vlPFC does not trigger the storage of information in AC on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential latency data.

claim: The storage in auditory cortex of information about sounds over several seconds may be an essential component of the analysis of temporal patterns of sounds including speech and communication sounds.
source: The storage in AC of information about sounds over several seconds may be an essential component of the analysis of temporal patterns of sounds including speech and communication sounds (May et al., 2015; Petkov and Jarvis, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The memory trace carried by persistent activity changes remains relatively unaltered throughout the memory period.
source: Because the change of the neural activity persisted throughout most of the period during which information needed to be stored, it is conceivable that the memory trace carried by this activity remains relatively unaltered throughout the memory period.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of persistent activity changes.

claim: Very similar persistent working memory-related activity was observed in the auditory cortex of humans and monkeys.
source: Because very similar persistent WM-related activity was observed in our studies in the AC of humans and monkeys, the cellular bases of some auditory WM processes in humans can well be studied in monkeys.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results from human and monkey studies.

claim: Fifteen subjects participated in study 1 and twenty-six in study 2.
source: Fifteen subjects (7 males, 8 females, mean age = 26 years) participated in study 1 and twenty-six (14 males, 12 females, mean age = 27 years) in study 2.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Data from three subjects in study 1 and from 11 subjects in study 2 were excluded prior to analysis because of strong artifacts or technical problems during measurements.
source: Data from three subjects in study 1 and from 11 subjects in study 2 were excluded prior to analysis because of strong artifacts or technical problems during measurements.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: The frequencies of tones A and B were 1.5 and 1.6 kHz, respectively, in study 1.
source: The frequencies of tones A and B were 1.5 and 1.6 kHz, respectively.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: The tone duration was 100 ms and the stimulus-onset interval 2000 ms in study 1.
source: The tone duration was 100 ms and the stimulus-onset interval 2000 ms.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: Source strengths were analyzed for correct trials only, which comprised approximately 90% of trials in study 1.
source: Source strengths were analyzed for correct trials (∼90%) only.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data analysis procedures.

claim: In task 1, the strength of the regional sources seeded in the left and right auditory cortex increased in response to S1 and remained at a level higher than that before S1 throughout the entire delay.
source: Figure 2a and b show that in task 1, the strength of the regional sources seeded in the left and right AC increased in response to S1 and, throughout the entire delay, remained at a level higher than that before S1 (p<0.001, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: In study 2, the frequencies of A, B and C were set to 1.5, 0.789 and 2.85 kHz, respectively.
source: In both tasks, the frequencies of A, B and C were set to 1.5, 0.789 and 2.85 kHz, respectively.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: Source strengths were computed for correct trials only, which comprised approximately 95% of trials in study 2.
source: Source strengths were computed for correct trials (∼95%) only.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data analysis procedures.

claim: Activity in auditory cortex was stronger than before S1 throughout the entire delay in both task 4 and task 5.
source: As in study 1, activity in AC was stronger than before S1 throughout the entire delay (p<0.001, permutation test) in both the delayed-match-to-sample (task 4) and the sound-discrimination task (task 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data from study 2.

claim: The peak amplitude of the M100 component is strongly modulated by attention.
source: This suggests that levels of general attention in tasks 4 and 5 were similar during the presentation of S1 because the peak amplitude of the M100 component is strongly modulated by attention (Kauramäki et al., 2012; Woldorff et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two monkeys (L and C) were trained to perform tasks 1 and 6.
source: Two of them (monkeys C and L) were trained to perform tasks 1 and 6, on an identical set of four two-tone sequences (AA, AB, BA and BB) within the same experimental sessions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: The frequencies of tones A and B were 3 kHz and 1 kHz, respectively, in the monkey study.
source: The frequencies of tones A and B were 3 kHz and 1 kHz, respectively, and their sound pressure level was 67 dB SPL.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: In most sessions, the stimulus-onset interval between S1 and S2 was 1000 ms, resulting in an 800-ms delay.
source: The stimulus-onset interval between S1 and S2 was 1000 ms in most sessions, resulting in an 800-ms delay, defined as the interval from the offset of S1 to the onset of S2.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In some sessions, the stimulus-onset interval between S1 and S2 was 1300 ms, resulting in an 1100-ms delay.
source: In other sessions, it was 1300 ms, resulting in an 1100-ms delay.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Microelectrode recordings were made from core fields of the right auditory cortex and left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Microelectrode recordings of single-unit and multiunit activity and of local field potentials from core fields of the right AC and, later in separate experimental sessions, also from the left prefrontal cortex started once the monkeys responded correctly to each sequence in ≥65% of the trials in both tasks during 10 consecutive sessions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedures.

claim: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed in 15.1% of single units in task 1 and 10.5% in task 6.
source: Similar findings were obtained from the 152 single units isolated from the multiunit recordings, although significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed less often (15.1% in task 1; 10.5% in task 6; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-unit spike activity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios occurred in only one of the two tasks in 92% of single units and in both tasks in 8% of single units.
source: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios occurred in only one of the two tasks in the majority of the units and in both tasks in the minority of the units (65% vs. 35% for multiunits and 92% vs. 8% for single units; Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of single-unit spike activity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Significant ratios only in task 1 occurred more frequently in units with a best frequency of approximately 3 kHz than in other units.
source: Significant spike-rate ratios only in task 1 occurred more frequently in units with a best frequency of ∼3 kHz (2.67–3.37 kHz) than in other units (26.7% vs. 9.4%; p<0.05, chi-square test, one-tailed).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data in relation to best frequency.

claim: Significant ratios only in task 6 occurred more frequently in units with a best frequency of approximately 1 kHz than in other units.
source: Significant spike-rate ratios only in task 6 occurred more frequently in units with a best frequency of ∼1 kHz (0.89–1.12 kHz) than in other units (30.1% vs. 15.4%; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data in relation to best frequency.

claim: Significant high-/low-load spike-rate ratios during the delay were observed in 23.2% and 18.8% of recordings in tasks 1 and 6 with the 1100-ms delay.
source: Significant ratios during the final 500 ms of the 1100-ms delay (23.2% and 18.8% of 69 recordings in tasks 1 and 6) were observed slightly, but not significantly more frequently (p>0.05 for tasks 1 and 6, chi-square test, one-tailed) than during the final 500 ms of the 800-ms delay (17.7% and 15.3% of 124 recordings).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike activity data with different delay durations.

claim: 238 multiunits were recorded from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex during 70 sessions in which monkey C performed tasks 1 and 6.
source: We analyzed 238 multiunits recorded during 70 sessions in which the monkey performed tasks 1 and 6.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental data.

claim: Neurons in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex could discharge significantly more spikes during the delay of high- than of low-WM-load trials or vice versa.
source: Like in core fields of AC, neurons in vlPFC could discharge significantly more spikes (p<0.05, permutation test) during the delay of high- than of low-WM-load trials (Figure 6a) or vice versa (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike activity data from prefrontal cortex shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: In ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, spike rates frequently changed in low-WM-load trials, and sometimes even more strongly than in high-WM-load trials.
source: Spike rates also frequently changed in low-WM-load trials, and sometimes even more strongly than in high-WM-load trials (Figure 6f,g).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike activity data from prefrontal cortex shown in Figure 6f,g.

claim: The experiments were approved by the authority for animal care and ethics of the federal state of Saxony-Anhalt.
source: The experiments were approved by the authority for animal care and ethics of the federal state of Saxony-Anhalt (No. 28-42502-2-1129IfN), and conformed to the rules for animal experimentation of the European Communities Council Directive (86/609/EEC).
evidence: This is a factual statement about ethical approval.

claim: The studies were designed and conducted following the guidelines for basic MEG research in the field of neuroscience.
source: The studies were designed and conducted following the guidelines for basic MEG research in the field of neuroscience (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a factual statement about methodological standards, supported by a citation.

claim: Regional sources were seeded in the left and right auditory cortex based on the anatomical MR image of each subject's brain.
source: Neural activity in AC was estimated by determining the strengths of two regional sources. They were seeded in the left and right AC, respectively, based on the anatomical MR image of each subject's brain.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the MEG analysis procedure.

claim: Individual source waveforms were geometrically averaged across subjects to obtain the grand mean source waveforms.
source: To obtain the grand mean source waveforms, individual source waveforms were geometrically averaged across subjects, for reasons given elsewhere (König et al., 2015; Matysiak et al., 2013; Zacharias et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure, supported by citations.

claim: Two regional sources were modeled in the left and right auditory cortex, seeded at the border of Heschl's gyrus and planum temporale.
source: Separately for each subject and task, we modeled the neuronal sources underlying the magnetic field distribution around the peak of the M100 component evoked by S1 by two regional sources, one in the left and one in the right AC. These regional sources were seeded at the border of Heschl's gyrus and planum temporale (Näätänen and Picton, 1987).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the source modeling procedure, supported by a citation.

claim: Three pairs of regional sources were seeded in left and right central, frontal and occipital cortical areas to model background activity.
source: In addition, we seeded three pairs of regional sources roughly symmetrically in left and right central, frontal and occipital cortical areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to model background activity, that is, to exclude potential confounds from other brain areas.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the source modeling procedure.

claim: The position of A1 was estimated using the spatial distribution of the units' best frequencies and the penetration traces of the electrodes.
source: The position of A1 was estimated using the spatial distribution of the units' best frequencies and the penetration traces of the electrodes, i.e., electrodes passed through parietal cortex into the auditory cortex (Brosch et al., 2005; Kaas and Hackett, 2000).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the anatomical localization procedure, supported by citations.

claim: The ventrolateral prefrontal cortex was identified by its anatomical location and by the latency and selectivity of neuronal responses for complex auditory stimuli.
source: The vlPFC was identified by its anatomical location (below the principal sulcus and anterior to the arcuate sulcus; Romanski and Goldman-Rakic, 2002) and by the latency and selectivity of neuronal responses for complex auditory stimuli (animal and human vocalizations, natural sounds, man-made sounds, and white noise).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the anatomical localization procedure, supported by a citation.
